title: Security guards turnover is pushing some companies toward robots
excerpt: Asylon's robot dogs and drones are patrolling large facilities as the security industry faces a retention problem.
content_html:
Asylon Robotics, a robotics security company, deploys autonomous drones and robot dogs to patrol the perimeters of large properties. Think stadiums, manufacturing plants, and warehouses.

The robots make scheduled rounds, stream video to a remote operations center, and investigate alarms. If they detect unusual activity, a human checks the alert and decides whether to notify on-site guards.

Damon Henry, Asylon's CEO and cofounder, told Business Insider that his company charges about $120,000 to $170,000 a year, depending on patrol frequency. This "white glove security service" includes the robots, maintenance, software, and remote operators, he said.

"You compare that against the national average for a fully-loaded 24/7 guard shift is about a quarter million right now," he said. "So you get good ROI."

The financial return may propose an obvious case for replacing existing human labor. However, the security-guard workforce is also experiencing high turnover, creating openings that must be filled just to replace departing workers.

A retention crisis

About 1.3 million Americans work as security guards. Employment is projected to remain roughly flat through 2034. Yet the industry expects to produce more than 160,000 openings each year, almost entirely to replace departing workers, a July report from the UC Berkeley Labor Center said.

"I think it's a retention crisis," Enrique Lopezlira, director of the Labor Center's Low-Wage Work program and coauthor of the report, told Business Insider.

The report found that annual turnover in the investigation and security services industry, where security guards make up about nearly three-quarters of workers, reached nearly 89% in 2024, compared with 66% across the entire private sector. Turnover peaked near 99% in 2022.

The problem isn't necessarily a lack of people in the US who could become guards — Lopezlira said employers are struggling to retain workers for a low-paying job with inadequate training and higher safety risks.

The median security guard earns $18.70 an hour, and nearly 43% lack employer-sponsored or union-sponsored health coverage, the study said.

Robots take over the third shift

Henry, the Asylon CEO, said customers want to stay ahead of the curve by implementing automation and physical AI into their infrastructure.

The other problem Asylon's customers face is reducing what's called a "blackout period" — gaps in coverage that employers can't staff or keep staffed.

"Training them and staffing them is super inconsistent, and it's a big burden on the business," Henry said.

Asylon has roughly 25 customers with about 50 robot deployments across the country. Henry said that some have deployed Asylon's robots so they could leave an otherwise vacant guard post unfilled.

The bots handle some of the more repetitive tasks: circling a property's perimeter, maintaining a visible security presence, and determining whether an alarm warrants a human response. One human Asylon employee at a remote operations center supervises six to eight robots across multiple sites, Henry said.

At Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, one Asylon robot dog — a retrofitted quadruped from Boston Dynamics affectionately named Benzie — helps patrol the exterior areas of the 2 million-square-foot sporting venue. The impetus for bringing the robot was safety, Henry said.

"On third shift, they had security guards that were essentially walking the streets of downtown Atlanta," he said. With Benzie, guards can remain indoors until a physical response is needed.

Henry said theft and vandalism at the site went down to zero within the first couple of months of deployment and has remained that way since, he said.

A spokesperson for Mercedes-Benz Stadium did not respond to a request for comment.

Part of the appeal of the robots is to shift the risk. Security guards die on the job at more than twice the rate of workers overall, the Berkeley report found. Nearly two-thirds of the fatal injuries result from assaults and other violent acts.

"Technology and robots can shift the risk, not just the tasks," Lopezlira said, adding that removing a person from an isolated overnight patrol could reduce their exposure to violence.

Robots still need people

The robots are not yet outright replacing human guards. Sometimes they can't finish the patrol without human help.

Henry estimated that Asylon's robots can autonomously navigate about 90% of a typical patrol. Remote human operators may still need to step in when the machines encounter crosswalks, doorways, or other complex areas. In addition, every threat is still verified by a person.

"It's like self-driving cars," Henry said. "They're getting pretty good, but they're not quite there."

Some security bots can run into more fundamental problems. In 2024, San Antonio International Airport experimented with Knightscope's 420-pound roving security robot, designed to respond to door alarms and inspect workers' badges.

The airport employees found that the robot struggled to navigate crowds, focus its camera on badges, and provide reliable audio and video feeds, San Antonio Express-News reported in May. The airport ended the trial run in about a month.

A spokesperson for San Antonio International Airport declined to comment.

William Santana Li, CEO of Knightscope, declined to comment on San Antonio's operations and said the company's robots have operated autonomously for over 4.4 million hours. He said Knightscope has 434 clients in the US.

Even the most reliable robot can only automate part of a guard's work. Human security guards, for example, de-escalate conflicts or respond to people experiencing mental-health crises — all of which require situational judgments.

Lopezlira made the case that automating the repetitive tasks of a guard's work underscores the need for better training and working conditions if they'll only be needed for high-stakes situations.

"The realistic near-term effect is not that guards are replaced," he said. "The human role is going to be pushed toward those hardest, higher-stakes parts of the work."

blocks.html_en: • Robotics

sentences.en: Robotics
sentences.zh: 机器人技术

content_html_zh:
Asylon Robotics 是一家机器人安全公司，部署自主无人机和机器狗在大型物业周边巡逻。 想想体育场、制造工厂和仓库。

机器人按计划巡视，将视频传输到远程操作中心，并调查警报。 如果他们检测到异常活动，人员会检查警报并决定是否通知现场警卫。

Asylon 的首席执行官兼联合创始人达蒙·亨利 (Damon Henry) 告诉 Business Insider，他的公司每年收费约 12 万至 17 万美元，具体取决于巡逻频率。 他说，这种“白手套安全服务”包括机器人、维护、软件和远程操作员。

他说：“与全国平均水平相比，目前满载的 24/7 轮班值班人数约为 25 万。” “所以你可以获得很好的投资回报率。”

财务回报可能会为取代现有的人力提出一个明显的理由。 然而，保安队伍的流动率也很高，产生了必须填补的空缺，以取代离职的工人。

保留危机

大约有 130 万美国人从事保安工作。 预计到 2034 年就业率将大致保持不变。 然而，加州大学伯克利分校劳工中心 7 月份的一份报告称，该行业预计每年会产生超过 160,000 个职位空缺，几乎全部是为了取代离职工人。

“我认为这是一场保留危机，”劳工中心低工资工作项目主任、该报告的合著者恩里克·洛佩兹利拉（Enrique Lopezlira）告诉《商业内幕》。

报告发现，保安人员约占工人总数的近四分之三的调查和保安服务行业的年流动率在 2024 年达到近 89%，而整个私营部门的年流动率为 66%。 2022年营业额达到峰值接近99%。

问题不一定是美国缺乏可以成为警卫的人——洛佩兹利拉表示，雇主正在努力留住工人从事低薪工作，培训不足，安全风险较高。

研究称，保安人员的平均收入为 18.70 美元/小时，近 43% 的保安缺乏雇主资助或工会资助的健康保险。

机器人接管第三班

Asylon 首席执行官亨利表示，客户希望通过在其基础设施中实施自动化和物理人工智能来保持领先地位。

Asylon 客户面临的另一个问题是减少所谓的“停电期”，即雇主无法配备或留住员工的保险缺口。

“对他们的培训和人员配备非常不一致，这对企业来说是一个很大的负担，”亨利说。

Asylon 拥有大约 25 个客户，在全国部署了大约 50 个机器人。 亨利说，一些人已经部署了 Asylon 的机器人，这样他们就可以留下一个空置的岗哨。

这些机器人可以处理一些重复性较高的任务：环绕房产周边、维持明显的安全存在以及确定警报是否需要人工响应。 亨利说，远程操作中心的一名 Asylon 员工负责监管多个地点的六到八个机器人。

在亚特兰大的梅赛德斯-奔驰体育场，一只 Asylon 机器狗（波士顿动力公司的改装四足动物，被亲切地称为 Benzie）帮助巡逻这个 200 万平方英尺的体育场馆的外部区域。 亨利说，引入机器人的动力是安全。

“在第三班时，他们的保安基本上是在亚特兰大市中心的街道上行走，”他说。 有了 Benzie，警卫就可以留在室内，直到需要做出身体反应为止。

亨利表示，在部署的头几个月内，该地点的盗窃和破坏行为已降至零，此后一直保持这种状态。

梅赛德斯-奔驰体育场的发言人没有回应置评请求。

机器人的部分吸引力在于转移风险。 伯克利报告发现，保安人员因工作死亡的比例是工人总体死亡率的两倍多。 近三分之二的致命伤害是由袭击和其他暴力行为造成的。

洛佩兹利拉说：“技术和机器人可以转移风险，而不仅仅是任务。”他补充说，将一个人从隔离的夜间巡逻中转移出来可以减少他们遭受暴力的机会。

机器人仍然需要人

机器人尚未完全取代人类警卫。 有时，如果没有人类的帮助，它们就无法完成巡逻。

Henry 估计，Asylon 的机器人可以自主导航约 90% 的典型巡逻任务。 当机器遇到人行横道、门口或其他复杂区域时，远程操作员可能仍然需要介入。 此外，每一个威胁仍然由专人验证。

“这就像自动驾驶汽车，”亨利说。 “他们已经变得相当不错了，但还没有完全实现。”

一些安全机器人可能会遇到更根本的问题。 2024 年，圣安东尼奥国际机场试验了 Knightscope 的 420 磅重的流动安全机器人，旨在响应门警报并检查工作人员的徽章。

据《圣安东尼奥快报》五月份报道，机场工作人员发现该机器人难以在人群中导航、将摄像头聚焦在徽章上以及提供可靠的音频和视频源。 大约一个月后，机场结束了试运行。

圣安东尼奥国际机场发言人拒绝置评。

Knightscope 首席执行官 William Santana Li 拒绝对 San Antonio 的运营发表评论，并表示该公司的机器人已经自主运行了超过 440 万小时。 他说 Knightscope 在美国有 434 个客户。

即使是最可靠的机器人也只能自动化警卫的部分工作。 例如，人类保安可以缓和冲突或对经历心理健康危机的人做出反应——所有这些都需要情境判断。

洛佩兹利拉认为，如果警卫只在高风险情况下需要，那么将警卫重复性工作任务自动化，就需要更好的培训和工作条件。

“现实的近期影响并不是警卫被替换，”他说。 “人类的角色将被推向工作中最困难、风险最高的部分。”
